The brand supports 27,000 farmers cultivating 1.4 lakh acres of certified organic farmland across 71 clusters in 10 States. The brand has developed over 100 subcategories and 250 products to cater to an expanding target base. The sources do not provide specific details on flagship projects or case studies beyond these general descriptions.

# Better Marketing Optimization With FPP Led Tracking | 24 Mantra Organic | FMCG

Better Marketing Optimization With FPP Led Tracking | 24 Mantra Organic | FMCG

24 Mantra Organic is an established brand in the grocery and gourmet space, with a core focus on organic food products. Currently, the brand has developed over 100 subcategories and 250 products to cater to an expanding target base.

Their challenge: Expanding beyond the carved niche

The sources indicate that 24 Mantra, as a direct-to-consumer (D2C) brand, likely positions its products to offer cost-effectiveness and value for money. By cutting out the middleman, 24 Mantra can provide lower prices and better margins while maintaining product quality. The sources emphasize that D2C brands like 24 Mantra can communicate the cost-effectiveness of their products, ensuring reasonable pricing and highlighting the balance between price and quality to maintain positive consumer perceptions. However, specific pricing details for 24 Mantra are not provided in the sources.

In traditional models, brands sell to retailers who markup products by 50-100% to sell to end customers.

If your product sells through a retailer for $10 per unit, you get $5, and your retailer gets $5. Conversely, if you sell that product directly to your customers on your website, you can sell it at $7.50 per unit, creating a higher profit margin and a lower price for the customer. It’s a win-win.

### More control over price [...] Price setting is a big part of your business strategy, but working with retailers makes it challenging. Adopting a direct-to-consumer approach gives you much more flexibility in this important area.

### Sell with your brand story, not just with your price and label design [...] When you work with a retailer, you can’t make last-minute price adjustments; you have to go through the proper channels.

Although D2C doesn’t mean that you can constantly change your prices, it does mean that you can run last-minute sales, add freebies to purchases, or instantly lower the price of a product that isn’t selling well.

# Communicating value beyond price

How do you balance affordability without cheapening your brand? In this lesson, learn how to plan a pricing strategy that compensates for margin compression and other market challenges.

When done correctly, brands can compete on tangibles like price. Since direct-to-consumer brands cut out the middleman by definition, the economics naturally enable brands to offer better price points for higher quality or distinctive products. [...] However, direct brands are as subject to commoditization pressures as indirect ones, making differentiation by function or price alone difficult. This strategy works only when coupled with a strong brand that speaks to consumers. But for many direct-to-consumer brands, that aspect comes easily. The hard part is developing a competitive pricing strategy that is sustainable at scale. [...] The same is true for moving into new channels — as a direct-to-consumer brand, this changes the total margin profile depending on the share of the business and costs per channel. There’s no blanket pricing change built in to these scenarios — you have to build a go-to-market strategy for each piece of the pie.

Consumers no longer only compare gains and losses in monetary terms but they measure the value of what they pay in terms of money, effort, and time against the product’s processes, features, quality (Kumar and Reinartz, 2016). Corresponding to this change, several DTC brand cases have shown high transparency, creating low-cost, high-quality, and high-value products. Therefore, we categorize the pricing factor in the DTC marketing model as: Cost-effectiveness. [...] - Reduce information asymmetry and enhance cost transparency. In the post-pandemic era, with economic slowdown and consumer downgrading, Brands should emphasize communicating the cost-effectiveness of products, ensuring reasonable product pricing, and highlight the balance between price and quality. They should aim to align cost management measures with conveying product value, allowing consumers to perceive value for money. This approach will maintain positive perceptions of product value and [...] - Cost-effectiveness | CE1 | Considering the price, I believe DTC brand products (services) are good. | Kim et al. (2021)
- CE2 | Regarding product quality, I find the prices of DTC brands to be good.
- CE3 | DTC brands offer reasonable quality and prices.
- Multi-channel Integration | Service construct transparency | TRA1 | Prior to making a purchase, I am acquainted with both the online and offline stores of DTC brands. | Sousa and Voss (2006)

Effective customer targeting starts with identifying and prioritizing the customer segments with the greatest commercial potential.
 Market segmentation combines demographic, psychographic, geographic, behavioral, and value-based approaches to create distinct and actionable customer groups.
 Value-based segmentation goes beyond traditional characteristics to understand what customers value, how their needs differ, and what drives their decisions. [...] Geographic segmentation divides the market based on location. It accounts for regional differences in tastes, needs, and cultural characteristics. This segmentation is crucial for businesses whose products or services vary in relevance and popularity across different regions.

 Behavioral segmentation. [...] The main approaches include demographic, psychographic, geographic, behavioral, needs-based, and value-based segmentation. The right approach depends on the business objective, available customer data, and the differences that meaningfully influence customer needs and purchasing behavior.

### What is value-based segmentation, and how does it differ from traditional segmentation?

24 Mantra differentiates itself through its extensive product range of over 200 organic food items, including grocery staples, vegetables, fruits, and traditional breakfast options with a variety of millets. It has a loyal customer base of more than 3 lakh households across 15 states in India and is available in over 1500 outlets. The brand emphasizes a farm-to-fork model, ensuring year-round availability and building trust through direct farmer engagement and traceability. It also opened its own stores in 2005 to build early consumer relationships. Recently, it has integrated into a larger FMCG ecosystem through its acquisition by ITC, which has brought stronger distribution, working capital support, and scale efficiencies.

The company has diversified further by introducing the Ready to Drink (RTD) and Ready to Cook (RTC) variants. The ready to cook variants comprises of Millet Dosa, Ragi Idly, Gojji Avalaki and Kanda Poha. With a loyal customer base of more than 3 lakh households across the country; 24 Mantra with its consistent quality is set to revolutionize our eating habits for the better. The products are available across 15 states with more than 1500 + outlets and even in US, UK.

[...] 24 Mantra has a product range of more than 200 + products comprising of grocery staples  – Grains, Pulses, Atta; vegetables, fruits , delicious cookies without Maida, assortment of teas and traditional breakfast options with a variety of millets etc.

To succeed, the brand had to ensure year-round availability for consumers. Even the distribution network had to be built from scratch. With mainstream retailers unwilling to stock an unproven category, the brand opened its own stores in 2005—a direct retail bet that proved critical to building early consumer relationships.

If awareness was the first barrier, trust quickly became the defining equity. [...] Seelam shared further, “Credibility had to be built internally—through direct farmer engagement, tighter control over sourcing, and investments in traceability. This focus on integrity became central to the brand’s positioning.” This translated into a QR-code-enabled supply chain allowing consumers to trace products to specific farms.

### From niche adoption to structural opportunity: ITC’s synergies [...] In recent years, the brand has seen a strategic pivot, with its integration into a larger FMCG ecosystem through its acquisition by ITC — bringing in stronger distribution, working capital support, distributed manufacturing and scale efficiencies while strengthening its core farm-to-fork model.

Instant grocery delivery, whose popularity has only shot up in this period, and organic foods are supposed to be a great pair. Neither is driven by discounts, and they both target affluent urban consumers.“It (organic foods) is a conviction-led category,” Sresta founder Rajashekar Reddy Seelam told The Ken. So, such brands finally have a distribution channel that isn’t price-sensitive supermarkets or fatigue-inducing e-commerce marketplaces. Now is as good a time as any for the likes of 24 [...] But a quick look at its numbers tell a different story. After a sharp rise in FY21, when consumers cooped up at home wanted to eat better, 24 Mantra’s annual sales have been largely flat since, at Rs 300–320 crore.
